title: Sustainability science

definition.text: An applied academic discipline, emerging in the 1980s, that studies sustainability and sustainable development and links knowledge to action.

facts.text: William C. Clark describes it as a field defined by the problems it addresses rather than the disciplines it uses.
It grew from publications such as the World Conservation Strategy (1980) and the Brundtland report Our Common Future (1987).
It was officially launched as an international field at a 2001 world congress in Amsterdam.
Recognising the epochal human impacts of the Anthropocene is at the core of much of the field.

definition.text: A holistic, interdisciplinary branch of ecology that studies ecosystems as complex systems, applying general systems theory to ecology.

facts.text: Its central idea is that an ecosystem is a complex system with emergent properties.
It is especially concerned with how human interventions affect ecosystem functioning, and so includes economics in studying ecological-economic systems.
A central feature is applying the principles of energetics to all systems at every scale; Howard T. Odum was its most notable proponent.
Ecological work deals almost entirely with open systems, which exchange with their surroundings across their boundaries.
Ecological engineering combines systems ecology with engineering design.

title: Maximum power principle

definition.text: Howard T. Odum's principle that organisms, ecosystems and societies organise themselves to maximise their use of available energy for survival.

facts.text: Odum held that societies with access to higher-quality energy had an advantage in the evolutionary struggle.
In systems ecology the principle of maximum power efficiency takes central place; the most advantageous function occurs when the environmental load matches the system's internal resistance.

notes: No crawled page of its own; mentioned on Steady-state economy and Systems ecology.

definition.text: The quantitative study of how energy flows through ecological systems.

facts.text: It looks for the principles governing energy flow through the trophic levels of ecological networks.
Systems ecology treats these 'ecosystem laws' as formally analogous to the principles of energetics.

title: Unequal exchange

definition.text: The hidden transfer of labour and ecological value from poor countries, mainly in the Global South, to rich countries and corporations, mainly in the North, through structurally unequal trade.

facts.text: Because of biased terms of trade, poor countries must export much more labour and resources than they import to keep trade in monetary balance.
It rejects the Ricardian and neoclassical claim that free trade based on comparative advantage benefits all parties.
Arghiri Emmanuel and Samir Amin traced it mainly to wage differences between core and periphery.
Hickel and colleagues calculated the drain from the Global South from 1990 to 2015 as equivalent to 242 trillion in 2010 US dollars.
Northern power is maintained partly through patents: 97% of all patents are held by corporations in high-income countries.
A common critique is that wage gaps reflect higher productivity in the North; supporters reply that productivity is measured by prices.

contested_note: Critics attribute North–South wage gaps to productivity differences, which unequal exchange theorists dispute.

definition.text: Raúl Prebisch's finding that prices of raw materials exported by poorer countries fall over time relative to the manufactured goods they import.

facts.text: Prebisch identified the pattern for Latin American exports such as coffee and copper while working for the UN Economic Commission for Latin America.
His ideas laid the foundation for dependency theory and import substitution industrialisation.
A recent study estimated that unequal exchange may have reduced North–South convergence by 34% across 43 countries between 2000 and 2014.

title: Human Ecology, Human Economy

definition.text: A 1997 book edited by Mark Diesendorf and Clive Hamilton combining human ecology and ecological economics to sketch an ecologically sustainable future.

facts.text: It was reviewed in Ecological Economics and The Australian Journal of Agricultural and Resource Economics.

notes: A single book, not a concept; excluded.
